neurological_exam.motor: Bulk normal throughout. Increased tone in both upper extremities with clear cogwheel rigidity at the right wrist and elbow, best elicited with activation (contralateral hand opening-closing); mild cogwheel component at the left wrist on reinforcement. Strength 5/5 in all extremities. No pronator drift. Bradykinesia evident on right-hand finger tapping with progressive decrement in amplitude and speed after 10 cycles; left hand shows mild slowing but substantially better amplitude maintenance.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch, pinprick, and proprioception intact in all extremities. Vibration mildly reduced at bilateral great toes (age-appropriate). No cortical sensory deficits.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally, patellar 2+ bilaterally, Achilles 1+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No Hoffmann sign. No clonus.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing accurate bilaterally without dysmetria; mild slowing on the right attributable to bradykinesia rather than ataxia. Heel-to-shin intact bilaterally. No cerebellar ataxia.
neurological_exam.gait: Gait mildly narrow-based with reduced right arm swing; left arm swing preserved. Stride length slightly shortened. En-bloc turning requiring 4 steps. neurological_exam.additional: A low-amplitude, approximately 4-5 Hz resting tremor is present in the right hand, most evident with the patient's hand resting quietly in his lap and during walking; the tremor diminishes with intentional movement and re-emerges after a brief latency on posture holding (re-emergent pattern). When both hands are outstretched, there is a moderate-amplitude bilateral postural and action tremor — more prominent on the left and present since the patient's 40s, consistent with his longstanding tremor history. Glabellar tap sign positive (fails to habituate after 10 taps). Handwriting sample shows early micrographia in the right hand. No myoclonus. Olfactory testing with the University of Pennsylvania Smell Identification Test (UPSIT): score 28/40, indicating mild hyposmia.

patient.chief_complaint: New right-hand resting tremor and progressive right-sided stiffness over the past 10 months, superimposed on a 20-year history of bilateral postural tremor
patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. Gerald Hartmann is a 64-year-old right-handed retired civil engineer who is referred to the neurology outpatient clinic by his primary care physician for evaluation of a new resting tremor in his right hand. He has a well-established, 20-year history of bilateral postural and action tremor that was diagnosed as essential tremor by his primary care physician in his mid-forties. This tremor has been largely stable and well controlled on propranolol 40 mg twice daily. He has noted throughout his life that one to two alcoholic drinks reliably and noticeably reduce the tremor — a feature his father and brother, who both have similar shaking, have also observed.

Approximately 10 months ago, his wife first noticed a new quality to his right-hand tremor: a slow, rhythmic trembling that occurred when his hand was resting in his lap while watching television, which was distinctly different from the postural tremor she had observed for years. The patient initially attributed this to a worsening of his essential tremor. Over the subsequent months, however, he has developed progressive stiffness and slowness affecting primarily the right side of his body. He finds it more difficult to button his shirt with his right hand, his right arm does not swing when he walks, and his handwriting has become smaller and less legible.

He also reports increased difficulty with fine manipulation tasks in his model railroading hobby, particularly with small parts requiring right-hand dexterity. His wife has noted that he occasionally seems to 'freeze' at the start of walking, and that he appears generally slower in all activities. He has had two near-falls while turning quickly over the past four months. He denies falls to the ground, visual hallucinations, cognitive decline, or urinary incontinence. He reports mild constipation over the past year, which he manages with dietary fiber. His wife has noted that he occasionally talks softly and moves his limbs during sleep over the past 8 months, which he was previously not doing.

The patient is concerned that he may simply have a worsening of his essential tremor, noting the strong family history of tremor (father, brother, maternal aunt) and his longstanding diagnosis. His primary care physician noted asymmetric cogwheel rigidity on examination and referred him for neurological assessment. He denies exposure to antipsychotic medications, antiemetics, or other dopamine-blocking agents. He denies head trauma, encephalitis, or toxin exposures.

results.title: DaTscan (Ioflupane I-123 SPECT) for differentiating Parkinson's disease from non-degenerative tremor disorders including essential tremor
results.key_finding: DaTscan reliably distinguishes presynaptic dopaminergic neurodegenerative disorders (PD, MSA, PSP) — which yield an abnormal scan — from essential tremor, drug-induced parkinsonism, and psychogenic tremor — which yield a normal scan. Sensitivity and specificity for detecting dopaminergic deficit exceed 90% in multicenter studies.

results.title: MDS Clinical Diagnostic Criteria for Parkinson's Disease
results.key_finding: Clinically established PD requires bradykinesia plus rest tremor or rigidity, with supportive criteria including levodopa response and olfactory loss. Essential tremor is a recognized mimic; the key discriminator is the presence of bradykinesia and cogwheel rigidity in PD (absent in pure ET) and, when uncertain, abnormal DaTscan (normal in ET, abnormal in PD).

results.title: Distinguishing essential tremor from Parkinson's disease: clinical features, DaTscan, and treatment response
results.key_finding: Features that distinguish PD from ET include: asymmetric rest tremor (re-emergent pattern), cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia, micrographia, reduced arm swing, and positive Myerson sign. ET is characterized by bilateral symmetric postural/kinetic tremor, alcohol responsiveness, and a positive family history — none of which exclude PD. DaTscan is the recommended ancillary test when clinical uncertainty exists; it is normal in pure ET regardless of family history or alcohol response.

interactions: Propranolol + levodopa: Propranolol (non-selective beta-blocker) may modestly attenuate the cardiovascular effects of levodopa and can reduce orthostatic compensation; monitor blood pressure on standing.
Amlodipine + levodopa: No clinically significant pharmacokinetic interaction; amlodipine may contribute to orthostatic hypotension — monitor standing BP after levodopa initiation.
contraindications: Non-selective MAO inhibitors (phenelzine, tranylcypromine): risk of hypertensive crisis; must be discontinued at least 14 days before starting levodopa. Patient is not on any MAO inhibitor.

Dopamine D2 receptor antagonists (typical antipsychotics, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine): would pharmacologically antagonize levodopa and can exacerbate parkinsonism. Patient is not on any dopamine antagonist.
warnings: Propranolol is an effective treatment for essential tremor; if a PD diagnosis is confirmed, propranolol will not address the parkinsonian rest tremor or bradykinesia — reassess tremor management accordingly.
Combined propranolol and levodopa may increase risk of orthostatic hypotension, especially at levodopa initiation; check lying/standing blood pressure.
Levodopa absorption may be reduced by high-protein meals; advise taking 30 minutes before meals.
Nausea is common early in levodopa therapy; a small carbohydrate snack at dosing may help without significantly reducing absorption.
Monitor for impulse control disorders and vivid dreams, particularly with dopamine agonists.

critical_actions: Apply MDS 2015 clinical diagnostic criteria: identify bradykinesia plus rest tremor on the right side as the cardinal parkinsonian features, distinct from the longstanding bilateral postural/action tremor

Recognize that a new asymmetric rest tremor with re-emergent pattern, unilateral cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia, micrographia, and hyposmia in a patient with prior ET diagnosis raises PD as a new, superimposed diagnosis

Order DaTscan to resolve the PD-vs-ET uncertainty — DaTscan is NORMAL in pure essential tremor and ABNORMAL in PD; the abnormal left putaminal deficit contralateral to the worse right-sided signs establishes PD
Check TSH to exclude hyperthyroidism as a reversible cause of tremor exacerbation
Review medications for dopamine antagonists before initiating levodopa; confirm propranolol interaction profile
Reassess propranolol utility: effective for the ET component but does not address parkinsonian rest tremor or bradykinesia; levodopa trial is indicated
contraindicated_actions: Do not label the patient as having 'worsening essential tremor' based solely on family history and alcohol responsiveness when asymmetric rest tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity, and an abnormal DaTscan are present
Do not prescribe metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, promethazine, or other dopamine D2 receptor antagonists for any indication in a patient with parkinsonism

Do not prescribe typical antipsychotics (haloperidol, fluphenazine) or high-risk atypicals (risperidone, olanzapine, aripiprazole) — restrict to quetiapine, clozapine, or pimavanserin if psychosis management is ever needed
Do not prescribe centrally acting anticholinergics (trihexyphenidyl, benztropine) in patients with even mild cognitive involvement or aged over 65
key_reasoning_points: Rest tremor with re-emergent pattern on posture holding, asymmetric cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia, micrographia, and hyposmia satisfy MDS 2015 parkinsonism criteria — these features are absent in pure essential tremor
Essential tremor and Parkinson's disease can coexist; a 20-year history of bilateral postural tremor does not exclude a new superimposed PD diagnosis

DaTscan is normal in pure essential tremor (regardless of severity, family history, or alcohol response) and abnormal in PD; this is the definitive discriminating test in cases of diagnostic uncertainty
The left posterior putaminal deficit on DaTscan is contralateral to the clinically worse right-sided parkinsonian signs — this is the expected lateralization in PD
A positive family history of tremor (father, brother, aunt) and alcohol responsiveness are classic ET red herrings; they do not identify the disease type when parkinsonism is also present
Hyperthyroidism is a reversible cause of tremor and should be formally excluded with TSH; in this case TSH is normal

red_herrings.data_point: 20-year history of bilateral postural and action tremor, diagnosed as essential tremor and treated with propranolol
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor the agent to an ET diagnosis and attribute all tremor, including the new rest tremor, to worsening ET rather than identifying a new superimposed parkinsonian disorder
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The new asymmetric rest tremor with re-emergent pattern, bradykinesia, and cogwheel rigidity are distinct from the longstanding ET; an abnormal DaTscan confirms a new presynaptic dopaminergic deficit consistent with PD

red_herrings.data_point: Strong family history of tremor (father, brother, maternal aunt all with 'shaky hands' or diagnosed ET)
red_herrings.intended_effect: Reinforce an ET attribution based on autosomal-dominant-appearing familial tremor pattern, discouraging consideration of PD
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Familial ET is a separate and common condition; family history of ET does not protect against or exclude PD; DaTscan is abnormal in this patient, establishing a presynaptic dopaminergic deficit

red_herrings.data_point: Alcohol responsiveness of tremor — patient reports that 1-2 drinks reliably and substantially reduce the tremor, dating back 15 years
red_herrings.intended_effect: Classic ET alcohol-response red herring — strongly suggest pure ET and discourage workup for PD
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Alcohol responsiveness reflects the longstanding ET component; it does not exclude PD, and does not apply to the newer parkinsonian rest tremor and bradykinesia; DaTscan is the discriminating test
